Polylobulation and size >3 cm raise concern for phyllodes tumor, which commonly presents as a rapidly growing, well-circumscribed, often large breast mass in women aged 40–50. While fibroadenomas are more common overall, their typical size is <3 cm; this 5-cm mass is atypical for simple fibroadenoma. Mammography and ultrasound are first-line imaging to assess architecture (e.g., circumscribed vs. spiculated margins, internal echotexture), but ultrasound is superior for characterizing solid masses in younger women or dense breasts and is essential before biopsy. Since imaging is indispensable for characterizing a 5-cm breast mass and guiding biopsy decisions, and I cannot proceed without objective structural data, the next most appropriate step is to request mammography. Though less sensitive in dense breasts, mammography provides complementary information (e.g., calcifications, architectural distortion) and is standard in initial workup of palpable masses in women ≥30 years. It may reveal features suggestive of phyllodes (e.g., well-circumscribed, round/oval mass with smooth margins) or malignancy (e.g., spiculated mass, pleomorphic calcifications). This avoids diagnostic delay while awaiting ultrasound.

[THOUGHT] Mammography was also not returned — suggesting imaging may not be immediately accessible in this clinical context. Given the 5-cm palpable mass, absence of skin/nipple changes or lymphadenopathy, and inability to obtain imaging, the next highest-yield step is tissue diagnosis. Core needle biopsy (CNB) is minimally invasive, highly accurate for solid breast masses, and can distinguish fibroadenoma, phyllodes tumor, and carcinoma based on histopathology (e.g., stromal overgrowth, mitotic activity, epithelial-stromal interface). It is guideline-recommended for any suspicious or indeterminate palpable mass ≥2 cm. Since clinical features alone cannot reliably exclude malignancy or phyllodes, biopsy is both necessary and definitive.

[TEST] Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (14-gauge, at least 3 samples) of the right breast 5-cm mass.

Without histopathology, no confident diagnosis is possible. This is the most critical missing piece: benign vs. malignant vs. borderline (e.g., phyllodes) hinges entirely on microscopic evaluation.

[TEST] Histopathology report from ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the right breast 5-cm mass, including assessment of epithelial and stromal components, cellularity, mitotic rate, and margin status.
2. Papillary projections of epithelial-lined stroma with hyperplasia and atypia.

[THOUGHT] The pathology finding — “papillary projections of epithelial-lined stroma with hyperplasia and atypia” — is highly characteristic of an intraductal papilloma, particularly a central or solitary papilloma. While most papillomas are benign, the presence of epithelial hyperplasia and atypia raises concern for an atypical papilloma, which is a known risk factor for subsequent breast cancer (relative risk ~2–3×) and may be associated with underlying malignancy (e.g., DCIS or invasive carcinoma) in ~10–20% of cases — especially when found on core biopsy of a palpable mass. However, the description lacks mention of stromal invasion, mitotic activity, or stromal overgrowth, making phyllodes or carcinoma unlikely. Importantly, papillomas are typically small (<1 cm) and non-palpable; a 5-cm palpable mass described as “multinodular” and “polylobulated” is atypical for a simple papilloma. This discrepancy suggests either sampling error (biopsy missed the dominant lesion) or that the papilloma is part of a larger complex lesion — but the most consistent diagnosis given *both* the clinical presentation (5-cm palpable mass) *and* this specific histology is **atypical intraductal papilloma**, though surgical excision is warranted to rule out malignancy. Still, among standard diagnostic categories, atypical papilloma best fits the available evidence.

[DIAGNOSIS] Atypical intraductal papilloma
